title: Big-O intuition
summary: Name how work grows: O(1), O(n), O(n²), and why constants are dropped.

steps.title: Big-O names the growth
body: Exact step counts like `3n + 7` are fussy and depend on how you count. **Big-O** keeps only the part that matters when `n` gets huge: the fastest-growing term, without its constant.
| `O(n)` | linear | one loop over the data | 1,000 |
| `O(n²)` | quadratic | a loop inside a loop | 1,000,000 |
So `3n + 7` is `O(n)` and `n² + 100n` is `O(n²)`: at a million items the `100n` part is a rounding error next to `n²`.

steps.prompt: Sort each snippet by how its work grows with `n` (the length of `a`).
items: two loops one after the other, each over `a`
steps.explain: Two loops **one after the other** cost `n + n = 2n`, still `O(n)`. Only loops **inside** each other multiply.

steps.prompt: An algorithm takes `5n² + 300n + 9` steps. What is its Big-O?
steps.explain: Keep the fastest-growing term (`5n²`) and drop its constant: `O(n²)`.

steps.title: Best case, worst case
body: Linear search stops as soon as it finds the target. Lucky input (target first) takes one step; unlucky input (target last, or missing) takes `n`.
Big-O normally describes the **worst case**, because that is the promise you can rely on.
Run the trace: the target `9` sits near the end, so `i` walks almost the whole array before `found` changes.

steps.prompt: Same search, new target. What does it print?
steps.explain: 7 is not in the array, so every element is checked: the worst case, `n` checks.

steps.prompt: An `O(n²)` routine takes 1 second for 1,000 items. Roughly how long for 2,000 items?
steps.explain: Doubling `n` squares into `(2n)² = 4n²`: four times the work. An `O(n)` routine would only double.

steps.prompt: Match each growth to what happens when the input doubles.

steps.title: From O(n²) to O(n)
prompt: `MaxDifference` returns the largest `a[j] - a[i]` over **any** two elements (order does not matter, so it is really `max - min`).
The starter is correct but compares every pair: `O(n²)`. The tests use an array of **200,000** numbers, which is 40 billion pairs, so it runs out of time.
Rewrite it to make **one pass**: track the smallest and largest value as you go. Keep the name and signature. Do not call `Min()`, `Max()` or sort.
template: Dojo.Eq("an empty array gives 0", 0, MaxDifference(new int[0]));
for (var dojoI = 0; dojoI < dojoBig.Length; dojoI++) dojoBig[dojoI] = (dojoI * 7919) % 100_003;
Dojo.Eq("200,000 numbers finish in time", 100_002, MaxDifference(dojoBig));

forbid.message: Does not call Min() or Max()

hints: Two variables, `min` and `max`, both starting at `a[0]`. Handle the empty array first.
One `foreach`: update `min` if `x` is smaller, `max` if `x` is larger. Return `max - min`.
